title: Insert Delete GetRandom O(1)
description:
# Insert Delete GetRandom O(1)

Implement the `RandomizedSet` class:

*   `RandomizedSet()` initializes an empty set.
*   `boolean insert(int val)` inserts `val` only if it is not already present. Return `true` when the value was inserted, otherwise return `false`.
*   `boolean remove(int val)` removes `val` only if it is present. Return `true` when the value was removed, otherwise return `false`.
*   `int getRandom()` returns a uniformly random value from the current set. Every value currently in the set must have the same probability of being returned. The set is guaranteed to be nonempty when this method is called.

Every operation must run in average `O(1)` time.

The example random return is one possible outcome; calls need not reproduce that exact value.

In operation examples, the first array lists operations and the second lists their argument lists, paired by index and executed left to right. The first operation constructs the object; later operations use that same object. Outputs align by index too: constructors and void methods produce `null`; an empty argument list `[]` means no arguments.

## Example 1:

**Input**
["RandomizedSet", "insert", "remove", "insert", "getRandom", "remove", "insert", "getRandom"]
[[], [1], [2], [2], [], [1], [2], []]
**Output**
[null, true, false, true, 2, true, false, 2]

**Explanation:** The first `getRandom` may return either `1` or `2` because both are present. After removing `1`, only `2` remains, so the final `getRandom` must return `2`.

## Constraints:

*   `-2^31 <= val <= 2^31 - 1`
*   At most `2 * 10^5` calls will be made to `insert`, `remove`, and `getRandom`.
*   There will be at least one element in the data structure when `getRandom` is called.

solutions.name: ArrayList Index Map
solutions.description:
## Approach

Store all current values in an `ArrayList<Integer>` and map each value to its current list index. Insert appends to the end. Remove finds the index, moves the last list value into that index, updates the moved value's index, and removes the tail. `getRandom` chooses a random dense index.

## Key Insight

Uniform random selection is easy only while the active values occupy a dense index range. Swap-remove preserves that dense range in O(1) average time while the map keeps removals from needing a scan.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(1) average per operation.
- Space Complexity: O(n).

solutions.name: Dynamic Int Array Index Map
solutions.description:
## Approach

Use a manually growing `int[]` for the dense values and a `HashMap<Integer, Integer>` for value-to-index lookup. The removal rule is the same swap-with-tail rule, but the dense storage avoids boxed list entries.

## Key Insight

This is the same invariant as the canonical route with a lower-level array implementation. It makes clear that the algorithm needs dense indexes, not a specific `ArrayList` API.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(1) average per operation; array growth is amortized.
- Space Complexity: O(n).

solutions.name: Dense Slot HashMaps
solutions.description:
## Approach

Emulate the dense array with two hash maps: `indexToValue` stores the value at each dense index, and `valueToIndex` stores the current index for each value. Removal swaps the last dense slot into the removed slot and updates both maps.

## Key Insight

The dense-index invariant can be maintained even without a physical array or list. This route is useful for explaining the two-way mapping needed by swap-remove.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(1) average per operation.
- Space Complexity: O(n).

solutions.name: Entry Object Dense Array
solutions.description:
## Approach

Store `Entry` objects in a dense `ArrayList`, and map each value to its `Entry`. Each entry stores its own current dense index. Removing an entry removes the tail entry and, when needed, writes that tail entry into the removed index while updating its stored index.

## Key Insight

Instead of updating a value-to-index integer directly, the moved object owns its index. This is a common design variant when the stored record has more fields than just the value.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(1) average per operation.
- Space Complexity: O(n).

solutions.name: Primitive Open Addressing Index Map
solutions.description:
## Approach

Use a dense `int[]` for current values and implement the value-to-index map with primitive open addressing arrays. Map states distinguish empty, occupied, and deleted slots. Removal marks the removed map slot as deleted and updates the moved tail value's stored index.

## Key Insight

The algorithmic invariant is still dense values plus value-to-index lookup. This route shows how the same idea can be implemented without Java's boxed `HashMap`, which matters when teaching the constant factors behind the O(1) claim.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(1) average per operation under the official call bound.
- Space Complexity: O(n).
